title: Round Hill is suing Suno and Anthropic for up to $1B apiece. It isn’t looking to settle.

reading.body:
The failure here is one of data acquisition and training scope. Suno admitted its model was trained on essentially all music files on the internet, and reporting based on a hack indicates the company scraped music from YouTube, Deezer, and Genius without obtaining licenses. The system was then deployed publicly in a state where it could reproduce passages closely matching specific copyrighted recordings, something the labels demonstrated by using targeted prompts and comparing outputs to songs they own.

This is a case of a generative model producing outputs that reproduce protected source material, a failure that originates in the training pipeline rather than in the inference stage alone. The gap between what the model could output and what rights the company held over its training data was never resolved before deployment. A rights-clearance check on training data, or output filtering against known copyrighted recordings, could have surfaced the problem earlier, but neither appears to have been in place.

What is not established is that any allegation of infringement, claim of intent to steal, or damages figure cited in lawsuits constitutes a legal finding. A German court ruled against Suno in the GEMA case, and a US court denied Suno's motion to dismiss artists' claims, but the broader US litigation involving record labels, class actions from independent artists, and suits from music publisher Round Hill remain unresolved. The settlements between Warner and Suno, and between Universal and Udio, resolved those specific disputes without producing findings on the underlying legal questions.

summary:
Major record labels including Universal Music Group, Sony Music, Warner Music, Capitol Records, and Atlantic Records have filed separate lawsuits against Udio and Suno, two popular artificial intelligence music generators. The labels accuse both companies of illegally scraping thousands of copyrighted songs without permission and directly reproducing sections of famous music in their AI-generated outputs. The lawsuits were filed in New York against Udio and in Massachusetts against Suno, the company headquarters locations. Both companies have refused to disclose which music trained their models, though they previously claimed their practices constitute fair use.

To support their cases, the record labels created a massive list of thousands of copyrighted works they claim were scraped, including catalogs from The Beatles, Michael Jackson, Mariah Carey, and many others. The labels demonstrated their evidence by using specific prompts on both generators and comparing the outputs to original songs they own. For example, prompting for "Mariah Carey, contemporary R&B, holiday" generated a near-identical version of "All I Want for Christmas Is You." The lawsuits set the stage for a major legal battle about how generative AI services can use copyrighted material during training.
